name: Hash Map Complement Lookup
triggers: Need to find whether a matching value was seen before.
Input is unsorted or sorting would destroy required output info.
Need original indices or prior values.
invariant: map[value] = index of a value already seen.
failureModes: Sorting when original indices matter.
Adding current value before checking complement and accidentally using the same element twice.
Using a plain object instead of Map when keys could be numeric or collide with object prototype.
contrastCases: Two Sum II: input is already sorted, so two pointers are valid.
3Sum: sort + fixed anchor + two pointers is better because output is values/triplets, not original indices.
intuition:
The complement lookup pattern exploits a mathematical relationship: if a + b = target, then for any a you encounter, b = target - a. The question becomes 'have I already seen b?' — which a hash map answers in O(1).

The key insight is the direction of the lookup. You don't search for pairs; you turn each element into a query against your memory. As you walk the array, you ask 'does my complement exist in what I've already seen?' If yes, you're done. If no, you record this element so a future element can find it.

This is why you check BEFORE inserting: you want to find a previously seen complement, not match an element with itself. Inserting first would let index 0 match index 0 if nums[0] * 2 === target.

complexity.explanation: Single pass over the array — O(n) time. In the worst case (no pair found until the last element) the map holds n-1 entries — O(n) space.

steps: i=0: need = 9 - 2 = 7. seen is empty → not found. Insert seen[2] = 0.
i=1: need = 9 - 7 = 2. seen has 2 → found! Return [seen[2], 1] = [0, 1].

whenNotToUse: Input is already sorted and you need original indices — Two Pointers gives O(1) space (but destroys index info if you sort an unsorted array).
You need all pairs, not just the first — the map approach returns immediately; you'd need to collect all matches instead.
Keys could be numeric strings or collide with Object.prototype — use Map, not a plain object.

name: Frequency Map / Count Array
triggers: Need counts of values or characters.
Need to compare multiplicity, not just existence.
Key space may be fixed, like lowercase English letters.
invariant: count[x] = number of unmatched occurrences of x.
failureModes: Using a Set when duplicates/counts matter.
Assuming alphabet size without checking constraints.
Using a plain object as a frequency map and hitting prototype-key collisions on unusual inputs.
contrastCases: Contains Duplicate: pure existence check — a Set is enough; no counts needed.
Group Anagrams: need the frequency as a canonical key, not just a count comparison.
intuition:
A frequency map answers one question: how many times did each value appear? The key insight is that two strings are anagrams if and only if they have identical frequency distributions — "anagram" and "nagaram" both produce {a:3, g:1, n:1, r:1, m:1}.

The trick that makes this O(n) instead of O(n²) is that counting is a one-pass operation. You iterate s once to build the counts, then iterate t once to cancel them out. If every count returns to zero, the distributions matched exactly.

When the key space is small and fixed (26 lowercase letters), you can use a plain array of size 26 instead of a Map — count[c.charCodeAt(0) - 'a'.charCodeAt(0)] — which is faster in practice because array access is cache-friendly and avoids hash computation.

complexity.explanation: Two linear passes over strings of length n. Space is O(1) because the count array is always size 26 regardless of input size — it is bounded by the alphabet, not the input.

steps: Early exit: both strings have length 7. Continue.
Pass 1 — count s: a→3, n→1, g→1, r→1, m→1. All other buckets stay 0.
Pass 2 — subtract t (n,a,g,a,r,a,m): n→0, a→2→1→0, g→0, r→0, m→0.
Final check: every bucket is 0. Return true — anagram confirmed.

whenNotToUse: Pure existence check (has anything repeated?) — a Set is enough; no counts needed. See: Contains Duplicate.
You need to group many strings by equivalence — use Canonical Key Grouping; the frequency array becomes the canonical key.
Unicode or multi-byte input — a fixed 26-slot array breaks. Use a Map keyed on the full character instead.

name: Two Pointers on Sorted Input
triggers: Input is sorted, or sorting is allowed.
Need pair/triplet relation like sum.
Moving one pointer has a monotonic effect.
whatItGives: O(n) scan after sorting or on already sorted input.
invariant: Current search space is between left and right. If sum is too small, move left. If sum is too large, move right.
failureModes: Using two pointers on unsorted input without monotonicity.
Sorting when original indices matter.
Incorrect duplicate skipping in 3Sum.
contrastCases: Two Sum: input is unsorted and you need original indices — use hash map instead.
Valid Palindrome: not sorted but still uses opposite-end convergence; non-alphanumeric skip complicates the loop.
intuition:
Two pointers work because sorted order gives you a guarantee: if you move the left pointer right, the sum goes up; if you move the right pointer left, the sum goes down. This monotonic property means you never need to revisit a position — each pointer moves at most n times, giving O(n) total.

Think of it as a search that uses the sort order to always make progress. If the current sum is too small, you need a bigger left element — move left forward. If the sum is too large, you need a smaller right element — move right backward. If the sum matches, you're done. You can never miss a solution because any skipped position is dominated by the current state.

The invariant is tight: the answer, if it exists, always lies within [left, right]. Once the pointers cross, all pairs have been considered.

complexity.explanation: O(n log n) if you need to sort first; O(n) if already sorted. Two-pointer scan is O(n) — each pointer moves at most n times total. O(1) space since only two indices are tracked.

steps: left=0 (val 2), right=3 (val 15). sum=17 > 9 → move right left.
left=0 (val 2), right=2 (val 11). sum=13 > 9 → move right left.

whenNotToUse: Input is unsorted and original indices matter — sorting destroys index info; use Hash Map Complement instead.
You need to find more than two elements — for 3Sum, anchor one element and run two pointers on the rest.
The 'move one pointer' step doesn't have a clear monotonic effect — two pointers only work when moving a pointer always changes the result in a predictable direction.

name: Sliding Window
triggers: Need best/valid contiguous subarray or substring.
Window validity can be updated incrementally.
Moving left can restore validity.
whatItGives: Usually O(n) because each pointer moves at most n times.
invariant: The current window satisfies the validity condition before updating answer.
failureModes: Updating answer before restoring validity.
Forgetting why nested while is still O(n): each pointer only moves forward.
Using final window state instead of global best.
contrastCases: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: single-pass greedy with implicit window — no explicit left/right shrink needed.
Frequency Map: counts chars but doesn't maintain a window boundary.
intuition:
A sliding window maintains a contiguous subarray or substring that satisfies some validity condition. The right pointer expands the window greedily; the left pointer shrinks it only when the window becomes invalid. Because each element enters the window once (via right) and leaves once (via left), the total work is O(n) even with a nested while loop.

The core insight is that validity can be maintained incrementally. You don't recompute the window from scratch each time — you update a counter or map as the window grows and shrinks. This is what makes the pattern efficient: O(1) update per step, not O(window size).

A common mistake is recording the answer inside the shrink loop instead of after it. The invariant must hold before you update your best. Always ask: is the window valid RIGHT NOW, and only then update the global best.

complexity.explanation: Each of the n characters enters the window exactly once (right pointer) and leaves at most once (left pointer) — O(n) total moves. Space is O(k) where k is the size of the character set tracked in the window map.

steps: right=0 ('a'): window=[a], freq={a:1}, no dup. best=1.
right=1 ('b'): window=[ab], freq={a:1,b:1}, no dup. best=2.
right=2 ('c'): window=[abc], freq={a:1,b:1,c:1}, no dup. best=3.
right=3 ('a'): freq[a]=2, dup! Shrink: remove s[left=0]='a', left=1. freq={a:1,b:1,c:1}. best=3.

whenNotToUse: The subarray doesn't need to be contiguous — sliding window only applies to contiguous windows.

Window validity can't be restored by moving the left pointer forward (e.g., sum problems where removing the leftmost element doesn't always restore validity) — re-examine whether a two-pointer or prefix-sum approach fits better.
You need the exact subarray, not just its length — track the left index at the time of the best result.

name: BFS Queue
triggers: Need shortest path in unweighted graph.
Need level order traversal.
Need to process nodes by distance/layers.
whatItGives: Processes nodes in breadth-first order; guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs.
invariant: Queue contains discovered nodes whose neighbors have not been processed yet. Mark visited when enqueuing, not when dequeuing.
failureModes: Marking visited on dequeue, allowing duplicate queue entries.
Queueing metadata instead of node labels.
Confusing graph node set with edge list.
contrastCases: DFS: explores one branch fully before backtracking — does not guarantee shortest path.
Level Order Traversal: snapshot queue length at start of each level to group nodes.
intuition:
BFS processes nodes in order of their distance from the source. Because a queue is FIFO, nodes enter in discovery order and leave in the same order — so all distance-1 nodes are processed before any distance-2 nodes. This layered processing is exactly what guarantees shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

The critical invariant is: mark nodes as visited WHEN YOU ENQUEUE THEM, not when you dequeue them. If you mark on dequeue, a node can be enqueued multiple times before it's processed, causing exponential work and incorrect results in dense graphs.

For level-order traversal, snapshot the queue length at the start of each level: the first `queueSize` dequeues belong to the current level. After processing all of them, increment the level counter.

complexity.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued once and dequeued once — O(V). Each edge is examined once — O(E). The queue holds at most one full level of nodes — O(V) in the worst case (a star graph where all nodes are at distance 1).

whenNotToUse: You need to explore one path fully before backtracking — use DFS instead.
The graph is weighted — BFS only gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; use Dijkstra for weighted.
Memory is constrained and the graph is wide — BFS stores an entire frontier level; DFS uses O(depth) stack space instead.

name: DFS Cycle Detection
triggers: Directed graph.
Need to know if a dependency cycle exists.
Shared subgraphs can be reused after proven safe.
whatItGives: Detects cycles in directed graphs using three-color DFS; also used for topological sort.
invariant: 0 = unseen, 1 = visiting / current recursion path, 2 = done / proven safe. Seeing state 1 means cycle.
failureModes: Using boolean visited for directed cycle detection.
Not distinguishing currently visiting from fully processed.
Building graph from edge list incorrectly.
contrastCases: BFS for cycle detection: works for undirected graphs but not directed.
Topological sort (Kahn's): BFS-based alternative using in-degree counts.
intuition:
To detect a cycle in a directed graph you need three states, not two. A boolean 'visited' isn't enough because it can't distinguish between 'currently on the recursion path' and 'already fully explored'. The three-color system captures this: 0 = unseen, 1 = currently visiting (on the stack), 2 = done (proven safe).

A cycle exists when DFS reaches a node with state 1 — you've looped back to something on the current path. When state is 2, you've already proven that subtree is cycle-free, so you can return immediately without re-exploring it. This is why three-color DFS handles shared subgraphs efficiently.

If you only have two colors, you can't tell whether a visited neighbor is an ancestor (cycle) or just a previously explored node in a different branch (no cycle). That ambiguity is exactly what state 1 vs state 2 resolves.

complexity.explanation: Each node transitions through states 0→1→2 exactly once — O(V). Each edge is examined once during DFS — O(E). Adjacency list storage is O(V + E).

steps: hasCycle(3): state[3]=1. No neighbors. state[3]=2. Return false.
Back at 2: state[2]=2. Back at 1: state[1]=2. Back at 0: state[0]=2.
No cycle found → return true (can finish).

whenNotToUse: The graph is undirected — a simpler boolean visited + parent-tracking DFS or union-find works.
You need topological order, not just cycle detection — extend this pattern by appending nodes to a result list after state[node]=2.
The graph has no directed edges — cycle detection is trivially true or false by inspection.

name: Set Membership
triggers: Question is pure existence: has anything repeated or appeared?
No counts needed — only presence/absence matters.
Need O(1) lookup for prior elements.
whatItGives: O(1) average membership test with minimal overhead.
invariant: set contains all previously seen values; membership test answers 'was this seen before?'
failureModes: Using a frequency map when only existence is needed.
Sorting to detect duplicates when O(n) Set solution suffices.
contrastCases: Frequency Map: use when counts matter, not just presence.
Hash Map Complement: use when you need to find a matching pair, not just any duplicate.
intuition:
A Set is the minimal data structure for existence queries. Its only job is to answer 'have I seen this before?' in O(1). When a problem only asks about presence — not count, not position, not order — a Set is always the right choice.

The pattern is almost mechanical: walk the collection, ask the Set if the current element is already there. If yes, you've found your duplicate (or match). If no, add it and continue. The Set grows as you walk, so you're always asking about the past.

The mistake beginners make is reaching for a frequency map or sorting when the problem doesn't require counts. Sorting is O(n log n) and destroys order; a frequency map is O(n) but carries overhead you don't need. When only existence matters, use a Set.

complexity.explanation: Single pass — O(n) time. In the worst case (no duplicates until the last element) the Set holds n-1 entries — O(n) space.

steps: i=0: seen = {}. 1 not in seen → add. seen = {1}.
i=1: 2 not in seen → add. seen = {1, 2}.
i=2: 3 not in seen → add. seen = {1, 2, 3}.
i=3: 1 IS in seen → return true.

whenNotToUse: You need to count how many times something appears — use a frequency Map instead.
You need to find a matching pair (e.g., two numbers that sum to target) — use Hash Map Complement.
The input is sorted — you can detect duplicates in O(1) space by comparing adjacent elements.

name: Canonical Key Grouping
triggers: Need to group elements that share some equivalence relation.
Two elements are equivalent if their sorted form or frequency signature matches.
Output is groups, not individual matches.
whatItGives: Groups equivalents in one pass using a derived canonical key.
invariant: All elements with the same canonical key map to the same bucket.
failureModes: Using sorted string as key without considering Unicode edge cases.
Building frequency array key with join separator that can collide across character positions.
contrastCases: Frequency Map: compares two strings directly; Canonical Key Grouping groups many strings.
Set Membership: checks existence; Canonical Key Grouping produces grouped output.
intuition:
Grouping requires a canonical key — a normalized form that all equivalent elements share. For anagrams, sorting the characters of a word always produces the same result regardless of letter order: 'eat', 'ate', and 'tea' all sort to 'aet'. Use that sorted form as the map key, and push each original word into the bucket at that key.

The power of this pattern is that you never compare two words directly. Instead, you derive a canonical representative and let the map handle the grouping. This generalizes beyond anagrams: any equivalence relation that can be expressed as a deterministic transformation produces a canonical key.

A subtle failure mode is key collision in frequency-array representations. If you use a comma-separated count array like '1,0,1,0,...' as the key, be careful that position 10 doesn't parse ambiguously with positions 1 and 0 adjacent. A separator like '#' between counts ('1#0#1#') avoids this.

complexity.explanation: For n words each of length at most k: sorting each word takes O(k log k), done n times. Space holds all words plus keys — O(n · k) total.

whenNotToUse: You only need to compare two strings — Frequency Map is simpler (no grouping needed).
The equivalence is not expressible as a string key — consider hashing or a different representation.
Unicode input — sort order may not be locale-independent; ensure consistent normalization.

name: Stack for Matching / Monotonic State
triggers: Need to match open/close pairs or nested structures.
Need to track the most recent unmatched element.
Monotonic property: answer depends on nearest larger/smaller element.
whatItGives: O(n) processing of nested or monotonic relationships.
invariant: Stack top is the most recent unmatched or relevant element; pop when a match or dominance condition is met.
failureModes: Popping without checking if stack is empty.
Forgetting to verify stack is empty at the end.
Using a queue instead of a stack (FIFO vs LIFO).
contrastCases: BFS Queue: FIFO; use for level-order traversal, not matching.
Min Stack: augmented stack for O(1) min queries — different from matching.
intuition:
A stack is LIFO — last in, first out. This mirrors nested structures perfectly: the most recently opened bracket must be the next one closed. When you see a closing bracket, you don't compare it against all previous opens — you compare it against the most recent unmatched open, which is exactly what the stack top gives you.

The invariant is: the stack always contains the unmatched opens in the order they appeared, most recent on top. When a close arrives, pop and verify. If they match, that pair is resolved and the stack top now represents the next unmatched open. If they don't match, it's invalid.

Don't forget the empty-stack check at the end: an empty string of opens with no corresponding closes leaves them all on the stack. A valid sequence leaves the stack empty.

complexity.explanation: Single pass over the n characters — O(n) time. In the worst case (all opens, no closes yet) the stack holds n/2 entries — O(n) space.

whenNotToUse: The structure is not nested — for flat pair matching, a counter may suffice.
You need FIFO order, not LIFO — use a queue instead.
You're looking for the minimum value in the stack — that requires an augmented Min Stack, not standard matching.

name: Tree DFS (Recursive)
triggers: Problem on a binary tree that can be solved per-node.
Answer at a node depends on answers from children (post-order) or parent context (pre-order).
Structural mutation or comparison of subtrees.
whatItGives: O(n) traversal with natural recursion; base case handles null nodes.
invariant: Each call returns the answer for its subtree; null returns the base-case value (0, true, null).
failureModes: Forgetting the null base case.
Confusing pre-order vs post-order when mutation order matters.
Returning a value that mixes subtree info with accumulated state.
contrastCases: BFS Queue: use when you need level-by-level processing, not depth-first.
Iterative DFS with explicit stack: needed when call-stack depth is a concern.
intuition:
Recursive tree DFS is elegant because the tree's structure mirrors the recursion's structure. Each call handles exactly one node: check the base case (null → return 0, true, or null), recurse into children, and combine results. The call stack implicitly tracks the path from root to current node.

The choice of traversal order matters: post-order (process children before the current node) is used when the answer at a node depends on its subtree — max depth, diameter, path sum. Pre-order (process current node before children) is used for structural mutations — invert, serialize, clone.

The null base case is the most important line. It handles both empty trees and the leaf-node-children case. Always handle null before accessing node.left or node.right.

complexity.explanation: Every node is visited exactly once — O(n). The call stack depth equals the tree height h — O(h) space. For a balanced tree h = O(log n); for a skewed tree h = O(n).

whenNotToUse: You need level-by-level processing — use BFS Queue instead.
The tree is very deep (n > 10,000) and the call stack could overflow — use iterative DFS with an explicit stack.
You need to track the path from root to node explicitly — pass a path parameter or use an iterative approach with a stack of (node, path) tuples.

name: Grid DFS / BFS Flood Fill
triggers: Grid of cells; need to count or process connected components.
Need to mark all reachable cells from a starting cell.
Trigger phrase: 'connected component count in a grid'.
whatItGives: O(rows × cols) traversal of all connected cells.
invariant: Once a cell is visited (marked or set to '0'), it will not be counted again.
failureModes: Marking visited after processing instead of before, causing infinite recursion.
Forgetting bounds checks before array access.
Using BFS without a visited set for grids where mutation is not allowed.
contrastCases: Clone Graph: graph nodes, not grid cells — use adjacency list + visited map.
Tree DFS: tree has no cycles; grid may have 4-directional neighbors.
intuition:
A grid is just a graph where each cell is a node and edges connect 4-directional neighbors. Flood fill is DFS (or BFS) from a source cell, marking all reachable same-value cells as visited by mutating them in place.

The key optimization is the in-place mutation: rather than maintaining a separate visited array, you overwrite the cell value as you visit it ('1' → '0' for Number of Islands). This means the visited check and the mark step are the same operation.

The recursion base case must check bounds and cell value BEFORE accessing the array. Wrong order causes index-out-of-bounds errors. The correct pattern: if out-of-bounds OR cell is not '1', return immediately.

complexity.explanation: Each cell is visited at most once — O(m × n) time. In the worst case (an all-land grid), the recursion depth is O(m × n) — O(m × n) call stack space. Use iterative DFS or BFS to avoid stack overflow on large grids.

steps: Outer loop: grid[0][0]='1' → count=1, call dfs(0,0).
dfs(1,0): mark '0'. Neighbors: dfs(2,0)→'0' skip, dfs(0,0)→'0' skip, dfs(1,1)→'0' skip. Return.
dfs(0,1): mark '0'. All neighbors '0' or OOB. Return.
Island 1 fully marked. Continue scan: grid[2][2]='1' → count=2.

whenNotToUse: The grid is very large — iterative BFS avoids recursion stack overflow.
You cannot mutate the grid — use a separate visited boolean array instead.
Nodes have arbitrary adjacency (not grid-based) — use general graph traversal with an adjacency list.

name: Prefix / Suffix Products
triggers: Need product of all elements except self.
No division allowed.
Answer at position i depends on all elements to its left and right.
whatItGives: O(n) solution without division by precomputing left and right running products.
invariant: result[i] = prefix[i] * suffix[i] where prefix[i] is product of all elements before i and suffix[i] is product of all elements after i.
failureModes: Trying to use division (fails when zeros are present).
Using O(n²) nested loop instead of prefix/suffix passes.
contrastCases: Running sum / prefix sum: for addition instead of multiplication.
Sliding window: for contiguous subarray problems, not element-exclusion products.
intuition:
The result at position i is the product of everything to i's left times everything to i's right. The challenge is computing that without using the element itself — and without division, which fails when zeros are present.

The insight is that you can precompute these two halves independently. A left-to-right pass builds prefix[i] = product of all elements before i. A right-to-left pass builds suffix[i] = product of all elements after i. Multiply them: result[i] = prefix[i] * suffix[i].

The space optimization is to merge the two passes: use the result array to accumulate the prefix product during the first pass, then multiply by a running suffix variable during the second pass. This avoids the separate prefix/suffix arrays, reducing space to O(1) beyond the output.

complexity.explanation: Two linear passes — O(n). The output array doesn't count as extra space per the problem convention. No intermediate prefix/suffix arrays needed — one running variable per pass.

steps: Pass 1 (prefix): result=[1,1,2,6]. result[i] holds product of all elements before i.
Pass 2 (suffix): suffix=1. i=3: result[3]*=1=6, suffix*=4=4. i=2: result[2]*=4=8, suffix*=3=12. i=1: result[1]*=12=12, suffix*=2=24. i=0: result[0]*=24=24, suffix*=1=24.

whenNotToUse: Division is allowed — you can compute total product and divide by each element (but still need special handling for zeros).
You only need a prefix sum, not product — simpler running sum suffices.
The problem is about a contiguous subarray — sliding window or Kadane's algorithm likely applies instead.

name: Heap / Top-K Selection
triggers: Need the K largest, K smallest, or K most frequent elements.
Need O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) full sort.
Problem mentions 'top K', 'K closest', or 'Kth largest'.
whatItGives: O(n log k) selection using a min-heap of size k.
invariant: Heap always contains the k best candidates seen so far; if new element beats the worst, replace it.
failureModes: Sorting the entire array when only K elements are needed.
Building a max-heap instead of min-heap for top-K (should evict the smallest).
contrastCases: Sort + slice: simpler but O(n log n); heap gives O(n log k).
QuickSelect: O(n) average for Kth element but harder to implement correctly.
intuition:
When you need the k best elements from n, sorting everything is wasteful — you're computing n - k rankings you'll throw away. A min-heap of size k is the right tool: it always evicts the worst of your current k candidates, keeping only the best k seen so far.

The invariant is: the heap contains exactly the k best elements seen so far, with the worst of those k at the top (easy to evict). For each new element, if it beats the heap's top (the current worst of the best k), swap it in. After processing all n elements, the heap holds the answer.

JavaScript has no built-in heap. For interview problems, the workaround is to build a frequency map and sort entries — O(n log n) but correct. For competitive settings, implement a min-heap or use bucket sort if values are bounded.

complexity.explanation: Each of the n elements is pushed/popped from a heap of size k — each heap operation is O(log k). Total: O(n log k). The heap holds at most k elements — O(k) space.

whenNotToUse: You need all elements sorted — use a full sort instead.
k = 1 — a single linear scan finds the max/min in O(n) with O(1) space.
You need the Kth element only (not the top K) — QuickSelect gives O(n) average without the heap overhead.

name: Backtracking
triggers: Need all subsets, permutations, or combinations.
Build solution incrementally; abandon a branch when a constraint is violated.
Output is a list of complete paths through a decision tree.
whatItGives: Explores all valid paths in the decision tree; prunes invalid branches early.
invariant: At each recursive call, the current partial solution is valid; after the call returns, undo the last choice (backtrack).
failureModes: Forgetting to pop/undo after the recursive call (corrupts shared state).
Using the same start index for permutations (should allow revisiting positions).
Missing the base case for Combination Sum (target becomes 0 or negative).
contrastCases: DP: memoize overlapping subproblems; backtracking enumerates all solutions.
BFS: explores by distance; backtracking explores by decision depth.
intuition:
Backtracking builds solutions incrementally and abandons a branch the moment it violates a constraint. Think of it as a depth-first search through a decision tree: at each node you make a choice, recurse, and when you return, undo that choice to explore the next option.

The critical discipline is the undo step — the 'backtrack'. Because you're mutating a shared path array, you must pop after each recursive call. Forgetting this is the most common bug: the path accumulates across recursive calls and the results are wrong.

For subsets, the decision at each step is 'include this element or skip it'. For combinations, you advance the start index to avoid reuse. For permutations, you mark elements as used. The shape of the decision tree depends on what's allowed — understanding that shape tells you exactly what to pass as parameters.

complexity.explanation: For subsets: each element is either included or not — 2^n subsets total. The call stack depth is at most n — O(n) space. Combination Sum has worse worst case depending on target/candidates ratio.

steps: bt(start=3, curr=[1,2,3]): push [1,2,3]. loop ends. return.
Back at [1,2]: pop 3. loop ends. return. Back at [1]: pop 2. recurse with 3.
bt(start=3, curr=[1,3]): push [1,3]. return. Back at [1]: pop 3. return. Pop 1.

whenNotToUse: You only need the count of solutions, not the solutions themselves — DP memoization is almost always faster.
The decision tree has overlapping subproblems — memoize with DP instead of re-exploring.
Constraints are tight and backtracking's exponential worst case would time out — consider greedy or DP.

name: 1-D Dynamic Programming
triggers: Optimal substructure: best answer for size n depends on best answers for smaller sizes.
Problem asks for count, min cost, or max value over a sequence.
Overlapping subproblems: naive recursion recomputes the same states.
whatItGives: O(n) bottom-up table fill after identifying the recurrence.
invariant: dp[i] holds the optimal answer for the first i elements (or up to position i); fill left to right.
failureModes: Off-by-one in the base case (dp[0] vs dp[1] meaning).
Using recursion without memoization, hitting exponential time.
Coin Change: forgetting to initialize dp with Infinity and handle unreachable states.
contrastCases: Backtracking: enumerates all paths; DP finds the optimal one.
Greedy: makes a local optimal choice; DP considers all subproblem outcomes.
intuition:
Dynamic programming applies when two conditions hold: optimal substructure (the best answer for size n can be built from best answers for smaller sizes) and overlapping subproblems (naïve recursion recomputes the same states). Memoization fixes the second; bottom-up DP avoids recursion overhead entirely.

For 1D problems, the state is usually a single index. You define dp[i] as 'the answer for the first i elements' and derive the recurrence — the formula expressing dp[i] in terms of earlier dp values. Then you fill the table left to right, using previously computed answers as building blocks.

The space optimization is recognizing that most 1D recurrences only look back 1 or 2 steps. Instead of a full dp array, two variables (prev1 and prev2) suffice, reducing space from O(n) to O(1).

complexity.explanation: Single pass over n elements, O(1) per step — O(n) total. With the two-variable optimization, only prev1 and prev2 are stored — O(1) space instead of O(n) for a full table.

steps: Recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) — either skip house i, or rob it and add to the best 2 houses ago.

whenNotToUse: No overlapping subproblems — pure recursion or greedy may be simpler.
You need all solutions, not just the optimal — backtracking enumerates solutions; DP finds the best one.
The state space is multidimensional (e.g., depends on two variables) — you need 2D DP, not 1D.

name: Binary Search
triggers: Search space is sorted or has a monotonic property.
Can determine which half to discard at each step.
Problem asks for minimum feasible value (binary search on the answer).
whatItGives: O(log n) search by halving the search space each iteration.
invariant: Answer always lies within [left, right]; after each step the range shrinks by at least half.
failureModes: Integer overflow: use mid = left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2), not (left + right) / 2.
Off-by-one: confusing left <= right vs left < right termination conditions.
Rotated array: not checking which half is sorted before deciding where to search.
contrastCases: Two Pointers: both pointers move; binary search only moves one boundary per step.
Binary search on answer: search space is the value range, not array indices.
intuition:
Binary search works on any search space with a monotonic property: some predicate that is false for the first part and true for the rest (or vice versa). Sorted arrays are the canonical example — elements to the left of the target are smaller, elements to the right are larger — but the technique generalizes to 'binary search on the answer' problems where the search space is a value range.

The invariant is: the answer always lies within [left, right]. At each step you compute mid and determine which half can be eliminated. If you can rule out the left half, set left = mid + 1. If you can rule out the right half, set right = mid - 1. The range shrinks by at least half each iteration — O(log n) total.

The most common bugs are integer overflow (use left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2), not (left + right) / 2) and off-by-one errors from confusing left <= right with left < right termination.

complexity.explanation: Each iteration eliminates half the remaining search space — O(log n) iterations. Only left, right, and mid are tracked — O(1) space.

whenNotToUse: The array is unsorted and sorting it would be too expensive or destroy required information.
You need all matching indices, not just one — binary search finds one; extend with a scan for duplicates.
The search space has no monotonic property — without a clear 'eliminate this half' rule, binary search doesn't apply.

name: Linked List Traversal / Manipulation
triggers: Input is a singly linked list.
Need to reverse, merge, or restructure node pointers.
Two-pointer (fast/slow) technique for cycle or midpoint detection.
whatItGives: O(n) in-place manipulation by rearranging next pointers.
invariant: At each step, maintain the invariant about which nodes are fully processed; never lose a reference before re-pointing.
failureModes: Losing the next pointer before saving it during reversal.
Not using a dummy head node for merge, causing extra null checks.
Reorder List: not finding the midpoint correctly before reversing the second half.
contrastCases: Array two pointers: random access; linked list must traverse sequentially.
Tree DFS: tree is a linked structure but with two children, not one next pointer.
intuition:
Linked list problems reduce to pointer manipulation — carefully rearranging next pointers without losing any references. The golden rule is: save next before you overwrite it. In reversal, this means const next = curr.next before curr.next = prev, otherwise you lose the rest of the list.

The dummy head node is the other essential tool. For merge and construction problems, starting with a dummy eliminates the special case of the first node — you always append to cur.next, so cur is never null. Return dummy.next at the end.

For finding the midpoint or detecting cycles, the fast/slow (Floyd's) pointer pattern runs one pointer at 2x speed. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the midpoint. This is the foundation for Reorder List: find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave.

complexity.explanation: A single pass over n nodes — O(n). Reversal and merge only track a constant number of pointers — O(1) extra space, in-place.

steps: prev=null, curr=1. Save next=2. Set 1.next=null. Move: prev=1, curr=2.
Save next=3. Set 2.next=1. Move: prev=2, curr=3.
Save next=4. Set 3.next=2. Move: prev=3, curr=4.
Save next=5. Set 4.next=3. Move: prev=4, curr=5.
Save next=null. Set 5.next=4. Move: prev=5, curr=null.
curr is null → done. Return prev (head of reversed list: 5→4→3→2→1).

whenNotToUse: Random access is needed — arrays support O(1) index access; linked lists require O(n) traversal.
You're tempted to convert to an array, process, then rebuild — this is often correct but O(n) space; check if in-place pointer manipulation is required.
The problem involves sorting — merge sort works on linked lists in O(n log n) but is complex to implement; consider if an array sort + rebuild is acceptable.

name: Graph Traversal (BFS/DFS on Adjacency List)
triggers: Input is a graph (not a tree, grid, or DAG for cycle detection).
Need to visit all reachable nodes from a source.
Need to clone, label, or count connected components in a general graph.
whatItGives: O(V + E) traversal of all reachable nodes and edges.
invariant: visited map/set prevents revisiting nodes; maps old node to new node for cloning.
failureModes: Not setting the clone in the map BEFORE recursing into neighbors (causes infinite loop on cycles).
Using node value as map key instead of node reference (fails with duplicate values).
contrastCases: Grid Flood Fill: cells in a grid; Graph Traversal: nodes with arbitrary adjacency.
DFS Cycle Detection: directed graph + three-color state; Graph Traversal: undirected reachability.
intuition:
General graph DFS/BFS adds one essential requirement over tree DFS: cycle prevention via a visited set. Trees are acyclic by definition — no node can be reached twice. Graphs can have cycles, so without a visited check you recurse infinitely.

For cloning, the visited map does double duty: it both prevents re-processing a node AND maps old nodes to their new copies. Setting the clone in the map BEFORE recursing into neighbors is critical — if a neighbor points back to this node (a cycle), the recursive call finds the already-created clone and returns it, rather than creating a second copy.

The subtle bug is using node.val as the map key instead of the node reference. If two nodes have the same value, they'd be treated as the same node, producing a corrupted clone.

complexity.explanation: Each node is cloned once and each edge is followed once — O(V + E). The visited/cloned map holds one entry per node — O(V) space.

steps: dfs(1): clone1 = {val:1, neighbors:[]}. cloned[1]=clone1 (set BEFORE recursing).
Recurse into neighbor 2: dfs(2): clone2={val:2}. cloned[2]=clone2. Recurse into 3.
dfs(4): clone4={val:4}. cloned[4]=clone4. Neighbor 1: cloned[1] exists → return clone1. Neighbor 3: cloned[3] exists → return clone3. clone4.neighbors=[clone1,clone3].
Back up the chain, each node's neighbors list is filled with the correct clones.

whenNotToUse: The input is a tree — tree DFS has no cycles, so the visited check and map are unnecessary overhead.
The graph is a grid — use Grid Flood Fill with in-place mutation instead of a separate map.
You only need reachability, not a full clone — a simple visited set and DFS/BFS loop suffices.
